CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should keep the door open to talks and avoid further tit-for-tat escalation, seeking to freeze or mitigate the scheduled January 2019 rise of List 3 tariffs from 10% to 25%. We have already retaliated proportionally ($34B + $16B + $60B), so we need not escalate again to save face; the priority now is to arrest a trade spiral that is already dragging down our export hubs and currency while preserving a firm negotiating posture. Engage Washington at senior level without new concessions, signaling willingness to increase purchases in exchange for pausing the January escalator, while preparing targeted retaliation if talks fail.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high (not yet existential). US Section 301 coverage has reached ~$250B of our exports across Lists 1/2/3 (timeline 2018-06-15, 2018-07-10, 2018-09-17, 2018-09-24), now roughly half our bilateral exports, and List 3 is threatened to rise from 10% to 25% in January — a material, imminent drag. Real-economy signs confirm the bite: Reuters polling (2018-10-16) forecast Q3 GDP at 6.6%, the weakest since 2009; manufacturing PMI stalled with export orders falling the most in over two years (CNBC 2018-10-01); Guangdong, our largest export province, reported lower exports in the first eight months; and the yuan has lost ~6% against the dollar, testing 7.0 with capital-outflow risk (Reuters/SCMP). Firm-level targeting (the ZTE denial order, timeline 2018-04-16) signals what a broader entity-list campaign could do to our tech sector, reinforcing the +0.6 reading just above the 'major export sectors hit / FX pressure / firm-level targeting' anchor — but not +1.0, since growth remains near the ~6.5% target, PBOC has cut RRR four times and has more room, reserves/controls are intact, and we have matched retaliation at each step.

The action stance is de-escalation-leaning negotiation rather than revenge. Escalating further would hand Washington the pretext to raise List 3 to 25% and broaden beyond $250B, worsening the export and currency damage our macro data already shows; a full capitulation, by contrast, would embolden further demands and erode domestic legitimacy. Negotiating to freeze the January escalator — while keeping retaliatory options ready — is the strategy that both limits self-harm and preserves leverage, hence action_score +0.1 and 'negotiate'.
key_factors: US Section 301 tariffs cover ~$250B of Chinese exports (Lists 1/2/3), with List 3 slated to rise from 10% to 25% on Jan 1, 2019
China growth decelerating: Q3 GDP forecast 6.6% (lowest since 2009); manufacturing PMI stalled ~50.0-50.8 with export orders falling fastest in 2+ years
FX/financial pressure: yuan ~6% weaker vs USD, probing 7.0, capital-outflow risk; Guangdong exports down YTD
Firm-level non-tariff targeting precedent (ZTE denial order) signals tech-sector escalation risk
China policy buffer: PBOC cut RRR four times, more easing latitude; reserves/capital controls intact; growth near ~6.5% target
China has already retaliated proportionally at each US tariff wave ($34B+$16B+$60B), so posture can stay firm without new escalation

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%; China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). Major non-tariff escalation.
China's third-quarter growth likely 6.6%, weakest since 2009; domestic demand faltering; exports front-loaded; yuan down ~6% this year; Guangdong exports down in first eight months.
Factory sector stalled after 15 months of expansion with export orders falling the most in over two years; official PMI at 7-month low of 50.8; PBOC likely to ease further.
Exports surged 14.5% in Sept partly on front-loading; record $34B bilateral surplus; real challenge 'next year' if tariffs extend.
